content: 1. A meta-analysis published in Chest in 2012 (Volume 142, Issue 1, Pages 63–75) evaluated the use of interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) and tuberculin skin testing to predict the progression from latent tuberculosis (TB) infection to active disease. 2. A consensus meeting report by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2017 outlined the development of a target product profile (TPP) and an evaluation framework for tests designed to predict the progression from TB infection to active disease. 3. Kik et al. (2018) proposed an evaluation framework for new diagnostic tests aimed at predicting the progression from latent TB infection to clinical disease, as published in the European Respiratory Journal (Volume 52, Issue 4). 4. The WHO issued a policy statement on the use of IGRAs in lowand middle-income countries, emphasizing their role in TB diagnosis. This document is available on the WHO website. 5. The 2019 Global Tuberculosis Report, published by the WHO, provides comprehensive data on the global burden of TB, including trends in incidence, prevalence, and mortality. 6. Ruhwald et al. (2017) conducted a phase 3, double-blind, randomized controlled trial comparing the safety and efficacy of the C-Tb skin test for diagnosing Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection with an IGRA and the tuberculin skin test. The findings were published in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine (Volume 5, Issue 4, Pages 259–268). 7. Barcellini et al. (2016) performed the first evaluation of the performance of the QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus assay in contact screening. The results were published in the European Respiratory Journal (Volume 48, Pages 1411–1419). 8. Getahun et al. (2015) outlined WHO guidelines for managing latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection in countries with a low TB burden. These guidelines were published in the European Respiratory Journal (Volume 46, Pages 1563–1576). 9. Nunn et al. (2019) conducted a clinical trial to evaluate a shorter treatment regimen for rifampin-resistant TB. The study was published in the New England Journal of Medicine (Volume 380, Issue 13, Pages 1201–1213). 10. Belknap et al. (2017) compared self-administered versus directly observed once-weekly isoniazid and rifapentine treatment for latent TB infection. The findings were published in Annals of Internal Medicine (Volume 167, Issue 10, Pages 689–697). 11. Watson and Petrie (2010) reviewed the correct methodology for method agreement analysis in diagnostic studies. Their work was published in Theriogenology (Volume 73, Pages 1167–1179). 12. The WHO guidance series for prequalification of diagnostic tools emphasizes the importance of establishing the stability of in vitro diagnostic medical devices. This includes examples of changes in key assumptions for sample size requirements to demonstrate the superiority of tests in terms of sensitivity and specificity. 13. Annex 1 of the WHO guidance provides examples of sample size calculations for demonstrating test superiority. For instance, a sensitivity improvement from 80% to 85% requires 1,164 participants, while a specificity improvement from 95% to 98% requires 233 participants. 14. Annex 2 outlines desirable operational characteristics for new in vitro TB diagnostic tests. These include minimal operator steps (preferably fewer than two), small sample volumes (especially for children, with a preference for pinprick over phlebotomy), and compatibility with digital data formats such as JSON for efficient result transmission and storage. 15. Training requirements for these diagnostic tools are minimal, with one day of dedicated training sufficient for non-laboratory-trained health personnel. This framework was adapted from the 2017 WHO consensus meeting report on TPP development for TB diagnostics.
